cells.tense: Right now the heart stays open and keeps its own shape.
cells.ask: Set down one thing you keep checking on, for a full day, and notice what still stands without you.
cells.core:
You can sit with someone and stay yourself. Their feeling reaches you, shifts the room a little, and doesn't erase where you end. Most people either hold back from that or go under it. You do neither, and you mostly don't notice you're doing it.

Since the ground is steady, there's room to loosen something small you've been gripping — a plan, a habit, a small certainty you keep returning to check. Pick one and see it through for a day. If it's still there after, you'll know it was yours to carry, not the grip that made it stay. If it isn't, you'll have found out something worth knowing. Letting go isn't the loss here. It's the clearing that shows you what the grip was actually for.
cells.sheetLine: You stay open and you stay someone. That's the whole skill.
cells.verb: feeling with someone without losing yourself, and letting go of what you no longer need to carry
cells.place: at the edge of what you've been holding, loosening your own grip on purpose

cells.tense: Before anyone has asked, you're already bracing to carry what they might need.
cells.ask: Tell one person a plain fact about your own day before asking about theirs.
cells.core:
You take on other people's states ahead of time. Their mood moves you before they've spoken, and you're already rearranging yourself to fit it. You call it caring, and some of it is — some of it is a grip that won't let anyone stand without your hands underneath them.

There's a small exit. Before you check on someone else, name one thing that's actually yours and let them hold it for a moment. Endings like this aren't losses; they clear the table. You don't have to stop caring. You can let a feeling belong to one person at a time, starting with you.
cells.sheetLine: You chose to hold on, and the hands are someone else's.

cells.tense: Arriving fully in a room with people stopped paying, and you're still at that door.
cells.ask: Choose one hour today, one person, one place, and spend the whole hour there.
cells.core:
The warmth is in there and it isn't reaching across the table. Conversations stay polite and shallow, your own included, and afterward you could not say what the other person cared about. It isn't cruelty. Standing at the door with your weight already back is simply how you've been showing up.

Closeness doesn't have to be pushed back in a flood. Start with where you're pointed: choose one hour today and spend the whole of it in one place with one person, phone off. A steady center shows up in company without having to perform warmth. One hour done fully tells you whether the connection is gone or just far away. Build the practice where you already are, not where you wish you were.
cells.sheetLine: You're here already, just decided halfway. Pick the whole place.

cells.tense: In this moment your hands are already on other lives in ways you would not claim.
cells.ask: Point at one thing that holds up someone's week and call that piece your own work.
cells.core:
Your life shows your care before you do. You remember what people need, you check in without being asked, you sit on the floor with a kid who needs it. Ask yourself directly and you would call all of that just being practical. Yes, and it is also your hands in the shape of other lives.

Here is what to test. Pick one thing other people lean on that runs because of you — call it infrastructure or whatever it is to you. Say plainly it's yours. Notice it's a pattern you can point at, not a background condition you're in. Whatever else it was, you folded a real feeling into a schedule so well you lost the address. Look at one small proof and let it be called love.
cells.sheetLine: Your hands are on other lives. You just called it being practical.
